attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, introduced with 'I predict'.

semantics.note: 'I predict... is going to' is a firm forecast with no deadline. 'At least one company' and the causal link to overreliance on AI are both kept. The 'perhaps' examples only illustrate the claim and do not hedge it.

contract.note: The plain reading is ordinary and fair: after the post, a publicly reported chain of AI-caused errors with embarrassing consequences such as a refund, retraction, legal loss or withdrawal. It is not stretched for or against him. The bar is low, but he set it with 'at least one company'.

evidence.note: AP, 2025-10-07: Deloitte partially refunded the Australian government over a report with apparent AI-generated fabrications, after public exposure. The chain of events falls after the post.
The revised report disclosed that Azure OpenAI was used to write it. This links the errors to reliance on AI.

Air Canada was held liable for its chatbot's advice in a February 2024 ruling. But the chatbot's error dates from 2022, before the post, so this is only partial fit and does not settle the claim alone.
Deloitte did not confirm that AI caused the errors. This weakens the causal link slightly, but AI use was disclosed and AP calls the errors apparently AI-generated.

reviews.rationale: The forecast has no deadline but meets its early-resolution rule. AP (2025-10-07, before the evaluation date) reports that Deloitte's government report contained apparent AI fabrications. AI use was disclosed, the errors were publicly exposed, the report was revised, and Deloitte made a partial refund. Deloitte did not confirm AI caused the errors, but the AI disclosure and the reporting meet the contract's standard of a credible source. Air Canada is context only, because its error predates the post.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The present-tense claim about AI's state in 2023 is kept accurately. The aside 'nor do I believe it will be for some time' is a separate, vague forecast with no deadline. Leaving it out is appropriate and does not change this claim.

contract.note: 'Realistically replace' is read as producing usable professional scripts without human writers. That is the ordinary reading in the context of the WGA strike. The period from May to 2023-08-03 is reasonable for 'currently'.

evidence.note: THR, May 2023: futurist Amy Webb judged AI could not effectively replace striking writers on most projects. At most it might produce a partial draft that humans would finish.
THR, May 2023: a talent lawyer said AI was not an existential threat to writers 'today'. This is weaker, indirect support.
AFP, May 2023: a Fox executive bullish on AI put its full creative ability years away, implying it could not do this in 2023.
Studios apparently believed AI could do the work, but a belief is not demonstrated capability. Neutral context.

reviews.rationale: Sources from inside the period, including a studio-side executive, agree that AI in mid-2023 could not realistically replace professional writers. The packet shows no production that replaced writers with AI. All the evidence is from May 2023 rather than July or August, but nothing suggests capability changed materially before the post date. On the fair plain reading, the observation is supported.
